title: Convergence of damped best responses in Tullock contests with no minimum effort
shortTitle: Contest learning without a minimum effort
oneLine: In Tullock contests with convex costs, players who repeatedly move part of the way towards their best reply reach the unique equilibrium even when expensive players drop out, answering the zero-floor question left open by Elkind, Ghosh and Goldberg (2024).
abstract: In a Tullock (lottery) contest each player wins with probability equal to its share of total effort and pays a private convex cost. When every player repeatedly moves a common fraction of the way towards its best reply, Elkind, Ghosh and Goldberg (2024) proved convergence only under a positive minimum-effort floor, which prevents expensive players from withdrawing and so changes the equilibrium, and left the floorless case open. This candidate proves convergence with no floor: for sufficiently small constant steps (with geometric decay of the Nikaido–Isoda gap) and for every vanishing step sequence with divergent sum, from any finite start with at least two positive efforts, with nonsmooth costs and zero marginal cost at zero allowed. The new ingredient is that every player's combined rival effort stays above an explicit positive constant from an explicit time, even when individual efforts tend to zero. Harmonic steps give a gap of order 1/k, exactly of that order when a strictly inactive player starts with positive effort. Corollaries cover concave impact functions (with damping in impact units) and unit-elastic Cournot partial adjustment, and local thresholds 4/n and 8ab/(a+b)^2 show that any uniform step must shrink with the number of players and cost heterogeneity. The certified step is extremely conservative. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Damped simultaneous best responses x ← (1−α)x + α·b(x) converge to the unique equilibrium without any minimum-effort floor, for constant α ≤ α* (geometric decay of the Nikaido–Isoda gap) and for every α_k → 0 with Σα_k = ∞; costs may be nonsmooth and players may withdraw (Theorem 1, proof).
Every rival total s_i stays above δ = μ/(373248 M³) once the cumulative step reaches an explicit Λ, although individual efforts may tend to zero (Lemmas 3–4, Proposition 5, proof).
Harmonic steps give a gap of order 1/k; it is exactly of order 1/k when a strictly inactive player starts with positive effort (Theorem 1(3), Proposition 10, proof).
The theorem transfers to concave impact functions, including Tullock exponents 0 < r ≤ 1, when damping acts on impact (Corollary 11, proof).
Local stability needs α < 4/n for n identical linear players and α < 8ab/(a+b)² for two players, so no uniform step avoids shrinking with n and cost heterogeneity (Proposition 12, proof).
Open: a step guarantee of order 1/n with polynomial cost dependence; player-specific speeds; noisy responses.

narration: Contest learning without a minimum effort. An Evidence Press briefing. First, the setting. In many competitions, such as research races, lobbying or online contests, each participant wins a prize with a probability equal to its share of the total effort, and effort is costly. Economists call this a Tullock contest. Its equilibrium often has expensive participants spending nothing at all. A natural question is whether simple learning reaches that equilibrium. Suppose every player repeatedly moves part of the way towards its best reply to what the others are doing. A 2024 study proved that this works, but only if every player is forced to keep spending at least some fixed minimum, which stops expensive players from dropping out and so changes the game. The authors asked whether the minimum is needed. The main finding is that it is not. The process still converges to the unique equilibrium, including when some players withdraw completely, for small enough constant steps and for any slowly shrinking steps. The key fact is simple: each player's rivals, taken together, never stop competing. If the others' total effort becomes tiny, the leading player's best reply is also small, so it eases off and the others recover. The paper makes the threshold and the time this takes explicit, shows that the error can fall like one over the number of rounds, and shows that the step size must shrink as the number of players grows. The limits: the guaranteed step size is far too small to use in practice, all players must adjust at the same speed, and best replies must be exact. This is an anonymous, unrefereed candidate, checked by AI-assisted review only, not peer review. Published on 31 October 2026, its paper and evidence are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.
